claim: Cpeb4 mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in blood of sepsis patients in two independent GEO datasets (GSE65682 and GSE57065).
source: In two independent GEO datasets, we observed that Cpeb4 mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in blood, whereas the Cpeb1–3 mRNAs did not present major expression changes (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of two GEO datasets (GSE65682 and GSE57065) showing differential expression, as presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Cpeb1-3 mRNAs did not present major expression changes in blood of sepsis patients.
source: In two independent GEO datasets, we observed that Cpeb4 mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in blood, whereas the Cpeb1–3 mRNAs did not present major expression changes (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of GEO datasets showing no major changes in Cpeb1-3 expression, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The peripheral blood of sepsis patients displays an increased number of monocytes/macrophages.
source: The peripheral blood of sepsis patients displays an increased number of monocytes/macrophages, which are one of the immune cell populations that express higher Cpeb4 mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Monocytes/macrophages are one of the immune cell populations that express higher Cpeb4 mRNA levels.
source: The peripheral blood of sepsis patients displays an increased number of monocytes/macrophages, which are one of the immune cell populations that express higher Cpeb4 mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from immune cell lineages shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deconvolution analysis suggested that myeloid cells expressed higher levels of Cpeb4 mRNA during sepsis.
source: Moreover, deconvolution analysis suggested that myeloid cells expressed higher levels of Cpeb4 mRNA during sepsis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by deconvolution analysis of blood samples from sepsis patients, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cpeb4MKO mice did not show any major phenotype in homeostatic conditions.
source: To further explore the significance of this correlation, we generated a Cre-mediated knockout mouse line of Cpeb4 specific for myeloid cells (Cpeb4lox/loxLyz2Cre, hereafter referred to as Cpeb4MKO); of note, these mice did not show any major phenotype in homeostatic conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by characterization data of Cpeb4MKO mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cpeb4MKO mice displayed lower survival rates than wildtype controls upon LPS-induced endotoxic shock.
source: Upon challenging these mice with an intraperitoneal dose of LPS (for LPS-induced endotoxic shock), Cpeb4MKO mice displayed lower survival rates than the wildtype (WT) controls (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cpeb4MKO animals presented splenomegaly after LPS challenge.
source: Cpeb4MKO animals also presented splenomegaly (Figure 1C) and increased splenic levels of the cytokines Il6, Tnf, and Il1a (Figure 1D), key in septic response (Schulte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by spleen weight measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cpeb4MKO animals had increased splenic levels of the cytokines Il6, Tnf, and Il1a after LPS challenge.
source: Cpeb4MKO animals also presented splenomegaly (Figure 1C) and increased splenic levels of the cytokines Il6, Tnf, and Il1a (Figure 1D), key in septic response (Schulte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR measurements of cytokine mRNA levels shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Il6, Tnf, and Il1a are key cytokines in septic response.
source: Cpeb4MKO animals also presented splenomegaly (Figure 1C) and increased splenic levels of the cytokines Il6, Tnf, and Il1a (Figure 1D), key in septic response (Schulte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schulte et al., 2013.

claim: CPEB4 ablation in myeloid cells is linked to an exacerbated inflammatory response.
source: These results link CPEB4 ablation in myeloid cells to an exacerbated inflammatory response, which impaired their survival when faced with sepsis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing increased cytokine levels and splenomegaly in Cpeb4MKO mice.

claim: CPEB4 ablation in myeloid cells impaired mouse survival when faced with sepsis.
source: These results link CPEB4 ablation in myeloid cells to an exacerbated inflammatory response, which impaired their survival when faced with sepsis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the survival data from LPS-challenged Cpeb4MKO mice.

claim: Cpeb4 mRNA was transiently upregulated in BMDMs after LPS stimulation, peaking between 3 and 6 hr.
source: Time-course analysis showed that Cpeb4 mRNA (but no other Cpeb mRNA) was transiently upregulated, peaking between 3 and 6 hr after LPS stimulation (Figure 2A), followed by CPEB4 protein accumulation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR time-course data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No other Cpeb mRNA (Cpeb1-3) was transiently upregulated in BMDMs after LPS stimulation.
source: Time-course analysis showed that Cpeb4 mRNA (but no other Cpeb mRNA) was transiently upregulated, peaking between 3 and 6 hr after LPS stimulation (Figure 2A), followed by CPEB4 protein accumulation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR time-course data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CPEB4 protein accumulation followed Cpeb4 mRNA upregulation after LPS stimulation.
source: Time-course analysis showed that Cpeb4 mRNA (but no other Cpeb mRNA) was transiently upregulated, peaking between 3 and 6 hr after LPS stimulation (Figure 2A), followed by CPEB4 protein accumulation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CPEB4 protein was detected as a doublet, with the slow migrating band corresponding to the hyperphosphorylated, active form.
source: The CPEB4 protein was detected as a doublet, with the slow migrating band corresponding to the hyperphosphorylated, active form (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2016; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by lambda phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Guillén-Boixet et al., 2016.

claim: Isolated BMDMs from Cpeb4 total KO mice had no major defects in their differentiation or proliferation rates compared with WT BMDMs.
source: Isolated BMDMs from Cpeb4 total KO mice (hereafter, Cpeb4–/–) had no major defects in their differentiation or proliferation rates compared with WT BMDMs, based on marker genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of myeloid markers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phosphorylated CPEB4 accumulated during the late phase of the LPS response.
source: In contrast, and consistent with the observation that phosphorylated CPEB4 accumulated during the late phase of the LPS response, comparative transcriptomic analysis between WT and Cpeb4–/– BMDMs showed that most differences appeared 6–9 hr after LPS stimulation, during the resolution phase of the inflammatory response (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data showing CPEB4 phosphorylation over time.

claim: Most transcriptomic differences between WT and Cpeb4–/– BMDMs appeared 6–9 hr after LPS stimulation, during the resolution phase of the inflammatory response.
source: In contrast, and consistent with the observation that phosphorylated CPEB4 accumulated during the late phase of the LPS response, comparative transcriptomic analysis between WT and Cpeb4–/– BMDMs showed that most differences appeared 6–9 hr after LPS stimulation, during the resolution phase of the inflammatory response (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The transcriptomic profile of Cpeb4–/– BMDMs included increases in hypoxia, glycolysis, and mTOR pathways.
source: The transcriptomic profile of Cpeb4–/– BMDMs included increases in hypoxia, glycolysis, and mTOR pathways, all of which have been linked to pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization during sepsis (McGettrick and O'Neill, 2020; Shalova et al., 2015; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Hypoxia, glycolysis, and mTOR pathways have been linked to pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization during sepsis.
source: The transcriptomic profile of Cpeb4–/– BMDMs included increases in hypoxia, glycolysis, and mTOR pathways, all of which have been linked to pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization during sepsis (McGettrick and O'Neill, 2020; Shalova et al., 2015; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McGettrick and O'Neill, 2020 and Shalova et al., 2015.

claim: HIF1a levels were increased in Cpeb4–/– BMDMs at both protein and mRNA levels after 9 hr of LPS treatment.
source: Further, we confirmed that HIF1a levels were increased, both at protein and mRNA levels, after 9 hr of LPS treatment (Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F, 2G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Interferon, NOTCH or IL6 signaling pathways were affected in Cpeb4–/– BMDMs.
source: Interferon, NOTCH or IL6 signaling pathways were affected in the KO (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The levels of anti-inflammatory transcripts, such as Il10 mRNA, were reduced in Cpeb4–/– BMDMs.
source: Conversely, the levels of anti-inflammatory transcripts, such as Il10 mRNA, were reduced in the Cpeb4–/– BMDMs (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The absence of CPEB4 disrupts the development and resolution of the LPS-induced inflammatory response in myeloid cells.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the absence of CPEB4 disrupts the development and resolution of the LPS-induced inflammatory response in myeloid cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined transcriptomic and phenotypic data from Cpeb4–/– BMDMs.

claim: The 3′-UTR of Cpeb4 contains 17 repeats of the AUUUA pentanucleotide.
source: Since the peak of Cpeb4 mRNA followed similar kinetics to pro-inflammatory ARE-containing mRNAs, such as Il6 and Il1a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we searched the 3′-UTR of Cpeb4 for AREs; we found 17 repeats of the AUUUA pentanucleotide (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARE-containing transcripts are stabilized through HuR binding during the early phase of the LPS response.
source: ARE-containing transcripts are stabilized through HuR binding during the early phase of the LPS response and destabilized at later times by TTP binding.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HuR and TTP function in LPS response.

claim: ARE-containing transcripts are destabilized at later times by TTP binding.
source: ARE-containing transcripts are stabilized through HuR binding during the early phase of the LPS response and destabilized at later times by TTP binding.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HuR and TTP function in LPS response.

claim: The switch between HuR and TTP binding is regulated by the LPS-activated p38α MAPK, which is encoded by Mapk14.
source: The switch between these two ARE-binding proteins is regulated by the LPS-activated p38α MAPK, which is encoded by Mapk14 (Tiedje et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tiedje et al., 2012.

claim: Cpeb4 mRNA expression levels were reduced in LPS-treated p38αMKO macrophages.
source: Next, we analyzed BMDMs from myeloid-specific Mapk14 KO mice (Mapk14lox/loxLyz2Cre, hereafter referred to as p38αMKO) (Youssif et al., 2018) and found that Cpeb4 mRNA expression levels were indeed reduced in LPS-treated p38αMKO macrophages (Figure 3A), suggesting that Cpeb4 expression is controlled by the p38α-HuR-TTP axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cpeb4 expression is controlled by the p38α-HuR-TTP axis.
source: Next, we analyzed BMDMs from myeloid-specific Mapk14 KO mice (Mapk14lox/loxLyz2Cre, hereafter referred to as p38αMKO) (Youssif et al., 2018) and found that Cpeb4 mRNA expression levels were indeed reduced in LPS-treated p38αMKO macrophages (Figure 3A), suggesting that Cpeb4 expression is controlled by the p38α-HuR-TTP axis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Cpeb4 mRNA levels are reduced in p38αMKO macrophages.

claim: Treatment of WT BMDMs with the p38α inhibitor PH797804 reduced Cpeb4 mRNA expression.
source: This observation was confirmed by treating WT BMDMs with the p38α inhibitor PH797804 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cpeb4 mRNA levels decayed significantly faster in p38αMKO BMDMs compared to WT BMDMs after transcription inhibition.
source: To test whether p38α regulates Cpeb4 expression at the transcriptional or post-transcriptional level, we first inhibited transcription in LPS-treated WT and p38αMKO BMDMs; we found that Cpeb4 mRNA levels decayed significantly faster in the latter (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: HuR binding to Cpeb4 mRNA was strongly enriched after LPS treatment in WT BMDMs.
source: We observed that HuR binding to Cpeb4 mRNA was strongly enriched after LPS treatment in WT BMDMs but to a lesser extent in p38αMKO BMDMs, as seen in RNA-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating that this induced binding occurred in a p38α-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: HuR binding to Cpeb4 mRNA was enriched to a lesser extent in p38αMKO BMDMs compared to WT BMDMs after LPS treatment.
source: We observed that HuR binding to Cpeb4 mRNA was strongly enriched after LPS treatment in WT BMDMs but to a lesser extent in p38αMKO BMDMs, as seen in RNA-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating that this induced binding occurred in a p38α-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: HuR binding to Cpeb4 mRNA occurred in a p38α-dependent manner.
source: We observed that HuR binding to Cpeb4 mRNA was strongly enriched after LPS treatment in WT BMDMs but to a lesser extent in p38αMKO BMDMs, as seen in RNA-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating that this induced binding occurred in a p38α-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential HuR binding between WT and p38αMKO BMDMs.

claim: TTP binds to the Cpeb4 3′-UTR at 6 hr after LPS treatment.
source: We then analyzed recently published datasets from TTP immunoprecipitation (iCLIP) followed by genome-wide analysis of its associated mRNAs in LPS-stimulated BMDMs (Sedlyarov et al., 2016). We observed binding of TTP to the Cpeb4 3′-UTR at 6 hr after LPS treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) when the TTP protein levels were high (Figure 3E), as well as reduced decay rates of both Cpeb4 and Tnf mRNAs in macrophages from mice with a myeloid cell-specific TTP deletion (hereafter, TTPMKO) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by TTP iCLIP data from Sedlyarov et al., 2016, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: TTP protein levels were high at 6 hr after LPS treatment.
source: We then analyzed recently published datasets from TTP immunoprecipitation (iCLIP) followed by genome-wide analysis of its associated mRNAs in LPS-stimulated BMDMs (Sedlyarov et al., 2016). We observed binding of TTP to the Cpeb4 3′-UTR at 6 hr after LPS treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) when the TTP protein levels were high (Figure 3E), as well as reduced decay rates of both Cpeb4 and Tnf mRNAs in macrophages from mice with a myeloid cell-specific TTP deletion (hereafter, TTPMKO) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cpeb4 and Tnf mRNAs showed reduced decay rates in TTPMKO macrophages.
source: We then analyzed recently published datasets from TTP immunoprecipitation (iCLIP) followed by genome-wide analysis of its associated mRNAs in LPS-stimulated BMDMs (Sedlyarov et al., 2016). We observed binding of TTP to the Cpeb4 3′-UTR at 6 hr after LPS treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) when the TTP protein levels were high (Figure 3E), as well as reduced decay rates of both Cpeb4 and Tnf mRNAs in macrophages from mice with a myeloid cell-specific TTP deletion (hereafter, TTPMKO) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA decay data from Sedlyarov et al., 2016, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: MKK6-induced p38α activation was sufficient to increase Cpeb4 mRNA levels in U2OS cells.
source: To further analyze the contribution of p38α signaling to Cpeb4 mRNA stability, we used human osteosarcoma (U2OS) cells expressing the p38α MAPK activator MKK6 under the control of the TET-ON promoter (Trempolec et al., 2017). MKK6-induced p38α activation was sufficient to increase Cpeb4 mRNA levels in these cells, and this effect was reversed by treatment with p38α chemical inhibitors (Figure 3G) as well as by shRNA-mediated depletion of HuR (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from U2OS cells shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The effect of MKK6-induced p38α activation on Cpeb4 mRNA levels was reversed by treatment with p38α chemical inhibitors.
source: To further analyze the contribution of p38α signaling to Cpeb4 mRNA stability, we used human osteosarcoma (U2OS) cells expressing the p38α MAPK activator MKK6 under the control of the TET-ON promoter (Trempolec et al., 2017). MKK6-induced p38α activation was sufficient to increase Cpeb4 mRNA levels in these cells, and this effect was reversed by treatment with p38α chemical inhibitors (Figure 3G) as well as by shRNA-mediated depletion of HuR (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from U2OS cells treated with p38α inhibitors, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The effect of MKK6-induced p38α activation on Cpeb4 mRNA levels was reversed by shRNA-mediated depletion of HuR.
source: To further analyze the contribution of p38α signaling to Cpeb4 mRNA stability, we used human osteosarcoma (U2OS) cells expressing the p38α MAPK activator MKK6 under the control of the TET-ON promoter (Trempolec et al., 2017). MKK6-induced p38α activation was sufficient to increase Cpeb4 mRNA levels in these cells, and this effect was reversed by treatment with p38α chemical inhibitors (Figure 3G) as well as by shRNA-mediated depletion of HuR (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HuR-depleted U2OS cells shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The Cpeb4 mRNA was stabilized by HuR and destabilized by TTP.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the Cpeb4 mRNA was stabilized by HuR and destabilized by TTP, and that the demonstrated competitive binding (Mukherjee et al., 2014; Tiedje et al., 2012) of these two ARE-binding proteins to Cpeb4 mRNA is regulated by LPS-driven p38α activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing HuR-mediated stabilization and TTP-mediated destabilization of Cpeb4 mRNA.

claim: The competitive binding of HuR and TTP to Cpeb4 mRNA is regulated by LPS-driven p38α activation.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the Cpeb4 mRNA was stabilized by HuR and destabilized by TTP, and that the demonstrated competitive binding (Mukherjee et al., 2014; Tiedje et al., 2012) of these two ARE-binding proteins to Cpeb4 mRNA is regulated by LPS-driven p38α activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results and supported by citations to Mukherjee et al., 2014 and Tiedje et al., 2012.

claim: 1173 CPEB4-associated mRNAs were identified in untreated BMDMs by RIP-seq.
source: We identified 1173 and 1829 CPEB4-associated mRNAs in untreated and LPS-treated BMDMs, respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-seq data listed in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 1829 CPEB4-associated mRNAs were identified in LPS-treated BMDMs by RIP-seq.
source: We identified 1173 and 1829 CPEB4-associated mRNAs in untreated and LPS-treated BMDMs, respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-seq data listed in Supplementary file 2.

claim: CPEB4-associated mRNAs include previously described CPEB4 targets such as Txnip and Vegfa.
source: These included previously described CPEB4 targets such as Txnip or Vegfa, while negative controls such as Gapdh were not detected (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-seq coverage plots shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gapdh was not detected as a CPEB4-associated mRNA in RIP-seq experiments.
source: These included previously described CPEB4 targets such as Txnip or Vegfa, while negative controls such as Gapdh were not detected (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-seq coverage plots shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The 3′-UTRs of CPEB4 co-immunoprecipitated mRNAs were enriched in canonical CPE motifs.
source: The 3′-UTRs of the CPEB4 co-immunoprecipitated mRNAs were enriched in canonical CPE motifs (Piqué et al., 2008), which we previously described as CPEB4 binding elements (Afroz et al., 2014; Igea and Méndez, 2010; Novoa et al., 2010), as well as in CPEs containing A/G substitutions (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous work.

claim: The 3′-UTRs of CPEB4 co-immunoprecipitated mRNAs were enriched in CPEs containing A/G substitutions.
source: The 3′-UTRs of the CPEB4 co-immunoprecipitated mRNAs were enriched in canonical CPE motifs (Piqué et al., 2008), which we previously described as CPEB4 binding elements (Afroz et al., 2014; Igea and Méndez, 2010; Novoa et al., 2010), as well as in CPEs containing A/G substitutions (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CPE variants with A/G substitutions have been shown to be specifically recognized by the Drosophila ortholog of CPEB2-4 (Orb2).
source: These CPE variants have been shown to be specifically recognized by the Drosophila ortholog of CPEB2-4 (Orb2) (Stepien et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stepien et al., 2016.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of CPEB4 targets indicated an enrichment of mRNAs encoding for components of the LPS-induced MAPK pathways.
source: Gene Ontology analysis of CPEB4 targets indicated an enrichment of mRNAs encoding for components of the LPS-induced MAPK pathways (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CPEB4 targets include mRNAs that participate in anti-inflammatory feedback loops that negatively regulate the LPS response.
source: These targets included mRNAs that participate in anti-inflammatory feedback loops that negatively regulate the LPS response, consistent with the phenotype observed in Cpeb4–/– BMDMs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Gene Ontology analysis and the phenotype of Cpeb4–/– BMDMs.

claim: Dusp1, Il1rn, Socs1, Socs3, Zfp36, and Tnfaip3 mRNAs specifically co-immunoprecipitated with CPEB4.
source: Thus, Dusp1, Il1rn, Socs1, Socs3, Zfp36 (which encodes TTP), and Tnfaip3 mRNAs specifically co-immunoprecipitated with CPEB4 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-seq coverage plots shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CPEB4 binding to Txnip, Dusp1, and Il1rn mRNAs was validated by RT-qPCR.
source: CPEB4 binding to Txnip, Dusp1, and Il1rn mRNAs was further validated by RT-qPCR, using Gapdh as negative control (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP followed by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Socs1 mRNA levels were reduced in LPS-treated Cpeb4–/– BMDMs compared to WT BMDMs.
source: The functional importance of the CPEB4 association was confirmed by the observation that both the Socs1 mRNA (Figure 4F) and SOCS1 protein (Figure 4G) levels were reduced in LPS-treated Cpeb4–/– BMDMs compared to WT BMDMs.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SOCS1 protein levels were reduced in LPS-treated Cpeb4–/– BMDMs compared to WT BMDMs.
source: The functional importance of the CPEB4 association was confirmed by the observation that both the Socs1 mRNA (Figure 4F) and SOCS1 protein (Figure 4G) levels were reduced in LPS-treated Cpeb4–/– BMDMs compared to WT BMDMs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The levels of Dusp1, Il1rn, Socs3, Tnfaip3, and Zfp36 mRNAs were reduced in LPS-treated Cpeb4–/– BMDMs.
source: Likewise, the levels of the Dusp1, Il1rn, Socs3, Tnfaip3, and Zfp36 mRNAs were reduced in LPS-treated Cpeb4–/– BMDMs (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs displayed reduced stability in the absence of CPEB4.
source: To examine whether these changes in mRNA levels originated transcriptionally or post-transcriptionally, we measured the stability of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs in WT or Cpeb4–/– BMDMs stimulated with LPS and treated with actinomycin D to block transcription. Indeed, both Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs displayed reduced stability in the absence of CPEB4 (Figure 4I), showing a strong element of post-transcriptional regulation of the mRNA levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: After 3 hr of LPS treatment, the stability of a reporter with CPEs increased compared to the same mRNAs but with CPEs inactivated by point mutations.
source: To confirm that this effect was mediated by the presence of CPEs in the mRNA 3′-UTRs, we studied the stability of reporter mRNAs with or without CPEs in LPS-stimulated RAW264 macrophages. Indeed, after 3 hr of LPS treatment, the stability of a reporter with CPEs increased compared to the same mRNAs but with CPEs inactivated by point mutations (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: CPEB4 sustained the expression of anti-inflammatory factors post-transcriptionally at late times following LPS stimulation by binding to the corresponding mRNAs and promoting their stabilization.
source: Taken together, our results suggested that CPEB4 sustained the expression of anti-inflammatory factors post-transcriptionally at late times following LPS stimulation by binding to the corresponding mRNAs and promoting their stabilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing CPEB4 binding, reduced mRNA stability in Cpeb4–/– cells, and reporter assays.

claim: CPEB4-bound mRNAs in BMDMs were enriched in AREs.
source: Given that CPEB4 and its binding element, CPE, have opposite effects on mRNA stability as TTP and its binding element ARE, we explored what happens when both binding elements are present in the same 3′-UTR. We found that CPEB4-bound mRNAs in BMDMs were enriched in AREs (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 53% (102/193) of the TTP-bound mRNAs in BMDMs were also co-immunoprecipitated by CPEB4.
source: Conversely, 53% (102/193) of the TTP-bound mRNAs in BMDMs (Sedlyarov et al., 2016; Supplementary file 4) were also co-immunoprecipitated by CPEB4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B and data from Sedlyarov et al., 2016.

claim: At a genome-wide level, there is a linear correlation between the number of CPEs and the number of AREs present in the same 3′-UTR.
source: Indeed, at a genome-wide level, we observed a linear correlation between the number of CPEs (Piqué et al., 2008) and the number of AREs (Gruber et al., 2011) present in the same 3′-UTR (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The induction of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNA was reduced in Cpeb4–/– macrophages.
source: For example, the induction of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNA was reduced in Cpeb4–/– macrophages, but the expression of Cxcl1 or Ptgs2 mRNA remained unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression kinetics data comparing WT and Cpeb4–/– macrophages.

claim: The expression of Cxcl1 or Ptgs2 mRNA remained unaffected in Cpeb4–/– macrophages.
source: For example, the induction of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNA was reduced in Cpeb4–/– macrophages, but the expression of Cxcl1 or Ptgs2 mRNA remained unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression kinetics data comparing WT and Cpeb4–/– macrophages.

claim: In the absence of TTP, the Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs did not display major changes.
source: Conversely, in the absence of TTP, the Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs did not display major changes, while the Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA levels increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from TTPMKO macrophages.

claim: In the absence of TTP, the Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA levels increased.
source: Conversely, in the absence of TTP, the Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs did not display major changes, while the Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA levels increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from TTPMKO macrophages.

claim: Ccl2 and Cxcl2 mRNA levels were affected in opposite directions in both Cpeb4–/– and TTPMKO macrophages.
source: In a third group, mRNA levels (including Ccl2 and Cxcl2) were affected (in opposite directions) in both the Cpeb4–/– and TTPMKO macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from both Cpeb4–/– and TTPMKO macrophages.

claim: The 3′-UTRs of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs were more enriched in CPEs.
source: Interestingly, the 3′-UTRs of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs were more enriched in CPEs, those of Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA were enriched in AREs, and those of Ccl2 and Cxcl2 mRNA presented opposite ARE/CPE ratios.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of 3′-UTRs.

claim: The 3′-UTRs of Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA were enriched in AREs.
source: Interestingly, the 3′-UTRs of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs were more enriched in CPEs, those of Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA were enriched in AREs, and those of Ccl2 and Cxcl2 mRNA presented opposite ARE/CPE ratios.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of 3′-UTRs.

claim: The 3′-UTRs of Ccl2 and Cxcl2 mRNA presented opposite ARE/CPE ratios.
source: Interestingly, the 3′-UTRs of Socs1 and Il1rn mRNAs were more enriched in CPEs, those of Cxcl1 and Ptgs2 mRNA were enriched in AREs, and those of Ccl2 and Cxcl2 mRNA presented opposite ARE/CPE ratios.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of 3′-UTRs.

claim: The relative amount of CPEs or AREs in the 3′-UTR of an mRNA might modulate the relative contribution of TTP and/or CPEB4 to their stability.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesized that the relative amount of these two cis-acting elements (CPEs or AREs) in the 3′-UTR of an mRNA might modulate the relative contribution of TTP and/or CPEB4 to their stability impact of the RNA-binding protein.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed differential effects of CPEB4 and TTP depletion on mRNAs with different ARE/CPE ratios.

claim: The ratio between late time points (6–9 hr) after LPS stimulation was more pronounced for ARE-dominant than for CPE-dominant mRNAs.
source: In an expression kinetics analysis following LPS stimulation, we found that the ratio between late time points (6–9 hr), during which transcripts are differentially destabilized, was more pronounced for ARE-d than for CPE-d mRNAs; in contrast, no differences were observed at early time points (1–3 hr) or at late time points if the same mRNAs were classified only as a function of their number of AREs (Figure 5G and H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression kinetics analysis shown in Figure 5G, 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 5.

claim: No differences in expression ratio were observed at early time points (1–3 hr) between ARE-dominant and CPE-dominant mRNAs.
source: In an expression kinetics analysis following LPS stimulation, we found that the ratio between late time points (6–9 hr), during which transcripts are differentially destabilized, was more pronounced for ARE-d than for CPE-d mRNAs; in contrast, no differences were observed at early time points (1–3 hr) or at late time points if the same mRNAs were classified only as a function of their number of AREs (Figure 5G and H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression kinetics analysis shown in Figure 5G, 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Downregulated mRNAs (6 hr/9 hr ratio <0.5) had a lower ARE:CPE score than sustained mRNAs (ratio >0.5).
source: Next, we generated a list of 1521 ARE- and CPE-containing mRNAs (Supplementary file 6) and classified them according to their ratio at late time points after LPS stimulation (6–9 hr), as 'downregulated' (6 hr/9 hr ratio <0.5) or 'sustained' (ratio >0.5) mRNAs. Notably, the downregulated mRNAs had a lower ARE:CPE score (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ARE:CPE scores shown in Figure 5I and Supplementary file 6.

claim: No differences in ARE:CPE score were found when only the number of AREs were considered.
source: However, no differences were found when only the number of AREs were considered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ARE:CPE ratio, but not the number of AREs alone, correlated with differential mRNA expression patterns during the resolutive phase of the LPS response.
source: These results indicate that the ARE:CPE ratio, but not the number of AREs alone, correlated with differential mRNA expression patterns during the resolutive phase of the LPS response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined analysis of ARE:CPE scores and expression patterns.

claim: The presence of CPEs correlated with higher mRNA levels at late times after LPS stimulation in reporter assays.
source: Compared with the reporter without CPEs or AREs (null), the presence of CPEs correlated with higher mRNA levels at late times after LPS stimulation, and these levels were progressively reduced by the addition of AREs (increasing ARE:CPE score) (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Reporter mRNA levels were progressively reduced by the addition of AREs (increasing ARE:CPE score).
source: Compared with the reporter without CPEs or AREs (null), the presence of CPEs correlated with higher mRNA levels at late times after LPS stimulation, and these levels were progressively reduced by the addition of AREs (increasing ARE:CPE score) (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The number of AREs in the absence of CPEs had no significant impact on the reporter expression levels.
source: On the other hand, the number of AREs in the absence of CPEs had no significant impact on the reporter expression levels (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The combination of CPEs and AREs on mRNAs, together with the regulation of their trans-acting factors CPEB4 and TTP, modulates mRNA stability in a transcript-specific manner to fine-tune mRNA expression during the late phase of inflammatory processes.
source: These results confirmed that the combination of CPEs and AREs on mRNAs, together with the regulation of their trans-acting factors CPEB4 and TTP, modulates mRNA stability in a transcript-specific manner to fine-tune mRNA expression during the late phase of inflammatory processes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of expression analysis and reporter assays.

claim: Differential regulation of mRNA stability plays a pivotal role in the uncoupling between the expression of pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators.
source: Physiological inflammatory responses rely on both rapid induction and efficient resolution to avoid the development of diseases. Differential regulation of mRNA stability plays a pivotal role in the uncoupling between the expression of pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators and is key to engaging the negative feedback loops that switch off the inflammatory response (Schott et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schott et al., 2014 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Differential regulation of mRNA stability is key to engaging the negative feedback loops that switch off the inflammatory response.
source: Physiological inflammatory responses rely on both rapid induction and efficient resolution to avoid the development of diseases. Differential regulation of mRNA stability plays a pivotal role in the uncoupling between the expression of pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators and is key to engaging the negative feedback loops that switch off the inflammatory response (Schott et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schott et al., 2014 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Temporal control of inflammation resolution is regulated by CPEB4-mediated mRNA stabilization.
source: Our work points to temporal control of inflammation resolution as being regulated by CPEB4-mediated mRNA stabilization, which acts in a coordinated manner with the well-known TTP-driven destabilization of mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing CPEB4's role in stabilizing anti-inflammatory mRNAs.

claim: CPEB4-mediated mRNA stabilization acts in a coordinated manner with TTP-driven destabilization of mRNAs.
source: Our work points to temporal control of inflammation resolution as being regulated by CPEB4-mediated mRNA stabilization, which acts in a coordinated manner with the well-known TTP-driven destabilization of mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing coordinated regulation of CPEB4 and TTP.

claim: The opposing activities of positive (CPE) and negative (ARE) cis-acting elements in the mRNA 3′-UTRs, together with the regulation of their trans-acting factors CPEB4 and TTP, generate temporal stability profiles.
source: We propose that the opposing activities of positive (CPE) and negative (ARE) cis-acting elements in the mRNA 3′-UTRs, together with the regulation of their trans-acting factors CPEB4 and TTP, generate temporal stability profiles, which fulfill the functions needed in each phase of the inflammatory process.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental results.

claim: CPEB4 and TTP levels and activities could be integrated during the LPS response through cross-regulation at multiple post-transcriptional and post-translational layers.
source: Our results indicate that CPEB4 and TTP levels and activities could be integrated during the LPS response through cross-regulation at multiple post-transcriptional and post-translational layers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing multiple levels of regulation.

claim: Upon LPS stimulation, p38α MAPK signaling regulates TTP phosphorylation, causing a shift in the competitive binding from an equilibrium between HuR and TTP towards a HuR preference.
source: First, their activities are coordinately regulated by MAPK signaling pathways. Upon LPS stimulation, p38α MAPK signaling regulates TTP phosphorylation, causing a shift in the competitive binding from an equilibrium between HuR and TTP towards a HuR preference, which stabilizes Cpeb4 mRNA and promotes CPEB4 expression during the late phase of the LPS response.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about p38α regulation of TTP and HuR, combined with the results showing Cpeb4 mRNA stabilization.

claim: The shift towards HuR preference stabilizes Cpeb4 mRNA and promotes CPEB4 expression during the late phase of the LPS response.
source: First, their activities are coordinately regulated by MAPK signaling pathways. Upon LPS stimulation, p38α MAPK signaling regulates TTP phosphorylation, causing a shift in the competitive binding from an equilibrium between HuR and TTP towards a HuR preference, which stabilizes Cpeb4 mRNA and promotes CPEB4 expression during the late phase of the LPS response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the results showing HuR-dependent stabilization of Cpeb4 mRNA.

claim: ERK1/2 MAPK signaling, which is activated by LPS, controls the progressive accumulation of the active hyperphosphorylated form of CPEB4.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Guillén-Boixet et al., 2016.

claim: CPEB4 regulates its own mRNA, generating a positive feedback loop that contributes to the increased CPEB4 levels and activity at the late phase of the LPS response.
source: Moreover, CPEB4 regulates its own mRNA, generating a positive feedback loop that contributes to the increased CPEB4 levels and activity at the late phase of the LPS response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CPEB4 binds to its own mRNA.

claim: CPEB4 binds to the mRNA encoding TTP (Zfp36), adding a negative feedback loop that restores TTP activity during the late LPS response.
source: Additionally, CPEB4 binds to the mRNA encoding TTP (Zfp36), adding a negative feedback loop that restores TTP activity during the late LPS response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RIP-seq data showing CPEB4 binding to Zfp36 mRNA.

claim: ARE-dominant mRNAs are enriched for transcripts that encode pro-inflammatory cytokines, which are expressed during the early phase of the LPS response.
source: Accordingly, ARE-d mRNAs are enriched for transcripts that encode pro-inflammatory cytokines, which are expressed during the early phase of the LPS response (Anderson, 2010; Spasic et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2010 and Spasic et al., 2012.

claim: CPE-dominant mRNAs are enriched for transcripts that encode factors that contribute to inflammation resolution during the late phase of the LPS response.
source: In contrast, CPE-d mRNAs are enriched for transcripts that encode factors that contribute to inflammation resolution during the late phase of the LPS response, such as Socs1, Il1rn, Dusp1, and TTP itself.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Gene Ontology analysis and the identity of CPE-dominant mRNAs.

source: Based on these correlations, we propose that the decreased stability of these mRNAs in the absence of CPEB4 could explain the impaired inflammation resolution observed in Cpeb4MKO mice.
evidence: The claim is a proposed explanation based on the combined results.

claim: CPEB4 targets include negative regulators of MAPKs, which generate a negative feedback loop that limits the extent of the inflammatory response.
source: CPEB4 targets include negative regulators of MAPKs, which generate a negative feedback loop that limits the extent of the inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Gene Ontology analysis showing enrichment of MAPK pathway components among CPEB4 targets.

claim: CPEB4 was overexpressed in patients with sepsis.
source: Accordingly, we found that CPEB4 was overexpressed in patients with sepsis, while myeloid-specific Cpeb4MKO mice with LPS-induced septic shock had lower survival rates and a more exacerbated inflammation than WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by the microarray analysis of sepsis patient samples shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TTP KO mice have exacerbated LPS-induced shock.
source: Thus, TTP KO mice have exacerbated LPS-induced shock (Kafasla et al., 2014), HuR KO mice display inflammatory phenotypes (Kafasla et al., 2014), and p38α deletion in macrophages reduces the LPS response and renders mice more resistant to endotoxic shock (Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kafasla et al., 2014.

claim: HuR KO mice display inflammatory phenotypes.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kafasla et al., 2014.

claim: p38α deletion in macrophages reduces the LPS response and renders mice more resistant to endotoxic shock.
source: Thus, TTP KO mice have exacerbated LPS-induced shock (Kafasla et al., 2014), HuR KO mice display inflammatory phenotypes (Kafasla et al., 2014), and p38α deletion in macrophages reduces the LPS response and renders mice more resistant to endotoxic shock (Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kang et al., 2008.

claim: CPEB4's main function is to recruit the polyadenylation machinery and promote the elongation of the poly(A) tail of its target mRNAs.
source: Previous studies have shown that CPEB4's main function is to recruit the polyadenylation machinery and promote the elongation of the poly(A) tail of its targets mRNAs (Weill et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weill et al., 2012.

claim: The role of CPEB4 in macrophage mRNA stabilization during inflammation suggests that the length of the poly(A) tail is regulated by a dynamic equilibrium between cytoplasmic deadenylation and polyadenylation.
source: Thus, the role of CPEB4 in macrophage mRNA stabilization during inflammation suggests that the length of the poly(A) tail is not regulated by an unidirectional process (ARE-mediated deadenylation), but rather as the result of a dynamic equilibrium between cytoplasmic deadenylation and polyadenylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing opposing effects of CPEB4 and TTP on mRNA stability.

claim: The equilibrium between deadenylation and polyadenylation could be modulated, quantitatively and temporarily, by the relative numbers of CPEs and AREs.
source: Moreover, this equilibrium could be modulated, quantitatively and temporarily, by the relative numbers of CPEs and AREs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Chronic inflammation is a major cause of disease.

evidence: The claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inflammation resolution is in part directed by the differential stability of mRNAs encoding pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory factors.

claim: TTP-directed mRNA deadenylation alone cannot explain the variety of mRNA expression kinetics that are required to uncouple degradation of pro-inflammatory mRNAs from the sustained expression of anti-inflammatory mRNAs.

claim: The RNA-binding protein CPEB4 acts in an opposing manner to TTP in macrophages.
source: Here, we show that the RNA-binding protein CPEB4 acts in an opposing manner to TTP in macrophages: it helps to stabilize anti-inflammatory transcripts harboring cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements (CPEs) and AREs in their 3′-UTRs, and it is required for the resolution of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-triggered inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is the main finding of the study, supported by the combined experimental results.

claim: CPEB4 helps to stabilize anti-inflammatory transcripts harboring cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements (CPEs) and AREs in their 3′-UTRs.
source: Here, we show that the RNA-binding protein CPEB4 acts in an opposing manner to TTP in macrophages: it helps to stabilize anti-inflammatory transcripts harboring cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements (CPEs) and AREs in their 3′-UTRs, and it is required for the resolution of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-triggered inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results showing CPEB4 binding to and stabilizing mRNAs with CPEs and AREs.

claim: CPEB4 is required for the resolution of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-triggered inflammatory response.
source: Here, we show that the RNA-binding protein CPEB4 acts in an opposing manner to TTP in macrophages: it helps to stabilize anti-inflammatory transcripts harboring cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements (CPEs) and AREs in their 3′-UTRs, and it is required for the resolution of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-triggered inflammatory response.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phenotype of Cpeb4MKO mice showing impaired inflammation resolution.

claim: Coordination of CPEB4 and TTP activities is sequentially regulated through MAPK signaling.
source: Coordination of CPEB4 and TTP activities is sequentially regulated through MAPK signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results showing p38α-dependent regulation of Cpeb4 mRNA stability and ERK-dependent CPEB4 phosphorylation.

claim: CPEB4 depletion in macrophages impairs inflammation resolution in an LPS-induced sepsis model.
source: Accordingly, CPEB4 depletion in macrophages impairs inflammation resolution in an LPS-induced sepsis model.
evidence: The claim is supported by the survival and cytokine data from Cpeb4MKO mice.

claim: The counterbalancing actions of CPEB4 and TTP, as well as the distribution of CPEs and AREs in their target mRNAs, define transcript-specific decay patterns required for inflammation resolution.
source: We propose that the counterbalancing actions of CPEB4 and TTP, as well as the distribution of CPEs and AREs in their target mRNAs, define transcript-specific decay patterns required for inflammation resolution.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental results.

claim: The opposing mechanisms of CPEB4 and TTP provide a fine-tuning control of inflammatory transcript destabilization while maintaining the expression of the negative feedback loops required for efficient inflammation resolution.
source: Thus, these two opposing mechanisms provide a fine-tuning control of inflammatory transcript destabilization while maintaining the expression of the negative feedback loops required for efficient inflammation resolution; disruption of this balance can lead to disease.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Disruption of the balance between CPEB4 and TTP can lead to disease.
source: Thus, these two opposing mechanisms provide a fine-tuning control of inflammatory transcript destabilization while maintaining the expression of the negative feedback loops required for efficient inflammation resolution; disruption of this balance can lead to disease.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotype of Cpeb4MKO mice and the association with sepsis.
